# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The evolution of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been marked by successive technological refinements, from balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) and drug-eluting stents (DES) [1]. Although DES dramatically reduced restenosis and target-lesion revascularization, concerns persisted regarding permanent metallic caging, impaired vasomotion, chronic inflammation, and late stent thrombosis [2,3]. Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) were conceived to provide transient mechanical support and drug delivery, followed by complete resorption, theoretically restoring vascular physiology [4]. This review summarizes the rationale, clinical evidence, limitations, and future directions of BVS technology.

## Rationale and Device Characteristics

The conceptual appeal of BVS rests on "vascular reparative therapy"—temporary scaffolding during the period of greatest restenosis risk, with subsequent disappearance permitting restoration of vasomotion, late lumen enlargement, and freedom from a permanent foreign body [4,5]. The most extensively studied device, the Absorb everolimus-eluting bioresorbable scaffold (Abbott Vascular), comprised a poly-L-lactide (PLLA) backbone with a poly-D,L-lactide coating eluting everolimus [6]. PLLA degrades via hydrolysis into lactate, ultimately metabolized to carbon dioxide and water over approximately 2–3 years [7]. Other devices included the magnesium-based Magmaris scaffold and the Igaki-Tamai PLLA scaffold, the first BVS implanted in humans [8,9].

## Early Clinical Evidence

The ABSORB cohort A and B studies demonstrated feasibility, with serial imaging showing scaffold resorption and recovery of vasomotor function [10,11]. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) confirmed strut coverage and late luminal changes consistent with the bioresorption hypothesis [12]. These encouraging mechanistic findings spurred larger randomized trials [13].

## Randomized Trials and Meta-analyses

The pivotal ABSORB II, III, and Japan trials compared Absorb BVS with the Xience cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent [14,15,16]. ABSORB III met its primary noninferiority endpoint for target-lesion failure at one year [15]. However, longer follow-up revealed troubling signals: ABSORB II failed to show superiority in vasomotion and demonstrated greater late lumen loss, with increased device-related events [17]. Pooled patient-level meta-analyses consistently identified higher rates of scaffold thrombosis, particularly very late thrombosis beyond one year, compared with metallic DES [18,19]. The AIDA trial likewise reported significantly increased definite or probable scaffold thrombosis with BVS [20]. A comprehensive meta-analysis confirmed an excess risk of myocardial infarction and device thrombosis [21].

## Mechanisms of Failure

Investigations into scaffold thrombosis highlighted the role of thick struts (approximately 150 µm), which disrupted laminar flow and delayed endothelialization [22]. Malapposition, incomplete lesion preparation, and undersizing contributed to early events, while late discontinuities and intraluminal scaffold dismantling during resorption underlay very late thrombosis [23,24]. OCT studies documented uncovered and malapposed struts as substrates for thrombus formation [25]. These findings underscored the critical importance of optimal implantation technique [26].

## Technique Optimization and the PSP Protocol

Recognition that procedural technique strongly influenced outcomes led to the "PSP" approach: adequate lesion **P**reparation, appropriate **S**izing, and high-pressure **P**ostdilatation [26,27]. Registries suggested that meticulous PSP reduced adverse events, though it could not fully eliminate the inherent risk associated with thick polymeric struts [27]. Avoidance of small vessels and use of intravascular imaging became recommended practice during the device's clinical use [28].

## Market Withdrawal and Current Status

In light of accumulating safety concerns, the Absorb BVS was withdrawn from commercial sale in 2017 [29]. Nonetheless, the BVS concept remains scientifically valuable, prompting development of next-generation scaffolds with thinner struts, faster resorption, and improved mechanical properties, alongside magnesium-based alternatives that have shown more favorable preliminary safety profiles [8,30]. Ongoing efforts aim to retain the physiological benefits of resorption while mitigating thrombotic risk [30].

## Conclusion

BVS represented an ambitious paradigm shift toward transient coronary scaffolding and vascular restoration. Although early mechanistic data were promising, randomized trials and meta-analyses revealed an unacceptable excess of scaffold thrombosis and myocardial infarction with first-generation devices, leading to withdrawal of the Absorb scaffold. The experience offers enduring lessons regarding strut thickness, implantation technique, and the necessity of rigorous long-term evaluation. The future of bioresorbable technology hinges on iterative device improvements and disciplined clinical investigation before widespread adoption can be reconsidered.
